title: Leveraging  the Genetics of carotid stenosis for identifying novel risk factors and therapeutic opportunities
text:
Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the leading causal of morbidity and mortality in the United States. Veterans are
at higher risk than the general population and CVD is the number one cause of hospitalizations in the VA.
Atherosclerosis, narrowing of arteries due to plaque, causes CVD. It affects the coronary arteries of the heart
causing heart attack, the peripheral arteries of the leg causing debilitating leg pain and gangrene, and the carotid
arteries leading to the brain causing stroke. Current approaches to prevent and treat CVD treat all forms of
atherosclerosis the same. Genetic studies of coronary and peripheral artery disease have identified important
differences, suggesting a tailored approach will work better. Similar studies for carotid artery disease are lacking,
which prevents the full implementation of precision medicine approaches. The proposed study will use data from
the VA Million Veteran Program to identify genes associated with carotid stenosis and quantify the impact of
known and novel risk factors. It will help establish tailored therapy to treat carotid stenosis and prevent stroke.

title: Using Informatics and Natural Language Processing to Develop a Clinical Decision Support Tool to Improve Intimate Partner Violence Diagnosis by Dentists and Assess its Feasibility and Acceptability
text:
Dentists may be the first and only providers who intimate partner violence survivors seek care from for their
face, mouth, or teeth injuries. However, screening and diagnosis challenges exist. This study aims to leverage
health informatics to develop a clinical decision support tool to streamline IPV screening for dentists.

title: Investigating the Effect of Caspases and Anti-Viral Responses on KSHV Tumorigeniesis
text:
Kaposi’s sarcoma is a tumor caused by Kaposi’s sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV) in AIDS and
transplant patients, and it is currently poorly treatable. Manipulating the cellular antiviral response reduces viral
replication, which is necessary for tumor formation, pointing to a potential strategy for targeted therapy. Using a
new disease-relevant model of infection, we will investigate how these antiviral responses impact tumor-related
processes during KSHV infection and to what extent they can be leveraged as new Kaposi’s sarcoma
treatments.

title: Lymph Node Delivery in Transplantation
text:
The overall goal of this proposal is to develop a targeted delivery system for immunoregulatory molecules in
transplantation that increases their efficacy and diminishes their toxicity, thereby improving transplantation
outcomes.

title: Drosophila models of human mitochondrial diseases
text:
This project is to generate a reagent resource that enables the characterization and validation of Drosophila
models of human mitochondrial diseases. These reagents will facilitate immunolocalization and
immunoprecipitation and be used together with existing RNAi transgenic lines to validate fly models of human
mitochondrial diseases. As mitochondrial diseases affect multiple organs, our proposal is relevant to most NIH
institutes.

title: Establishing a National Consortium to Investigate Adaptive Immune Responses in Invasive Fungal Sinusitis
text:
Invasive fungal sinusitis is a devastating, highly morbid infection of the paranasal sinuses and the only current
surgical and medical treatment options have serious side effects. This study will investigate factors related to
both systemic immunity and host sinonasal tissue alterations that allow invasive fungal infection in vulnerable
patients. The long-term goal of this study is to develop targeted and improved therapies for this deadly
disease.

title: Defining the role of GNAS in gastrointestinal metastasis
text:
Patients with gastrointestinal (GI) cancers that metastasize to the peritoneal cavity suffer high morbidity and
mortality and have few effective treatment options. Mutations in the GNAS gene are associated with higher rates
of peritoneal metastasis, as well as decreased responses to chemotherapy in many GI cancers. The study will
investigate the impact of GNAS mutations on tumor molecular signaling cascades and tumor progression,
improve fundamental knowledge of tumor peritoneal metastasis, and evaluate GNAS inhibition as a new
promising treatment strategy for the large number of patients with metastatic GI cancers.

title: State-dependent Engineering of Therapeutic Functions in Reactive Astrocytes
text:
The specific inflammatory reactive astrocytes found at sites of neuropathology represent an ideal target for
localized therapies designed to minimize widespread side effects. Therefore, this project aims to develop a novel
RNA-based medicine, utilizing an "orthogonal RNA circuit" to reprogram this detrimental cell subtype for
therapeutic benefit.

title: Principles of Speckle-Based Gene Regulation
text:
Gene regulatory programs are critical drivers of poor outcomes across many disease states, yet the
role of nuclear speckles as fundamental drivers of regulatory programs is largely unexplored. By
tackling the principles of speckle-based gene regulation, the proposed research opens new therapeutic
avenues. Our work has particular implications for clear cell renal cell carcinoma and neuroblastoma, but
we anticipate that the principles uncovered can be applied across disease conditions.

title: Identifying molecular traits associated with extreme human longevity using an AI based integrative approach
text:
There is an urgent need for biomarkers of human aging. This project uses Artificial Intelligence to analyze data
from multiple genomic assays to identify novel biomarkers of aging, some of which have the potential to be
compelling targets of intervention.

title: Project 2: Functional Genetic Networks for Systems-Guided Precision Medicine
text: CCMI v2.0 Project 2: Functional Genetic Networks for Systems-Guided Precision Medicine Project Leads: Prashant Mali and Stephanie Fraley; Co-Investigators: Alan Ashworth, Jennifer Grandis, Silvio Gutkind, Trey Ideker, and Laura van ’t Veer. SUMMARY Precision medicine aims to tailor therapies to the genetic and molecular background of a patient’s tumor. The development of such therapies faces numerous obstacles, many deriving from our ignorance of the genetic networks underlying tumorigenesis and the mechanisms of possible interventions. To clarify the genetic logic that governs therapeutic efficacy, Project 2 will use CRISPR/Cas9 genetic perturbation methodologies in an ensemble of combinatorial, functional, and mechanistic screens. Screens will focus on the PI3K pathway, the p53 tumor suppressor, and the protein systems mutated in invasive breast cancer (BRCA), head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC), and lung squamous cell carcinoma (LUSC), pathways and diseases that together result in well over one million deaths each year worldwide. This focus will enable us to interrogate a broad collection of cell lines, experiments, and microenvironmental conditions. First, we will build on significant preliminary data to establish maps of synthetic lethal and epistatic genetic interactions centered on frequently mutated genes and therapeutic targets in the above pathways and cancer subtypes (Aim 1). Second, we will couple CRISPR/Cas9 screening to a panel of scalable functional assays for large-scale measurement of cancer phenotypes beyond cell proliferation (Aim 2). Third, we will pilot a new technology, STAG-CRISPR, to link CRISPR/Cas9 screening to real time molecular events in living cells, providing access to an even deeper array of phenotypes that have been recalcitrant to systems genetics thus far (Aim 3). Finally, to facilitate clinical translation of the identified gene-gene, gene-phenotype, gene-mechanism and gene-drug interactions, we will apply our extensive library of BRCA, HNSCC, and LUSC patient-derived xenograft (PDX) models to test compelling leads in vivo. We will also validate the identified interaction networks with patient data from the BRCA I-SPY 2 trial and from HNSCC patients at UCSD (Aim 4). Taken together, our integrated approach establishes a network of extensively validated interactions among genes, drugs and multiple phenotypic endpoints to advance the practice of precision oncology.

title: Socio-ecological factors linked to co-occurring early childhood sleep health disparities and developmental outcomes
text:
Sleep disordered breathing (SDB) and insufficient sleep are two highly prevalent sleep deficiencies in
preschoolers that frequently co-occur, disproportionately affect non-Latinx Black compared to non-Latinx White
youth, and negatively impact crucial neurobehavioral and social-emotional development. Modifiable family,
childcare, and neighborhood factors that contribute to or buffer against these sleep health disparities and their
developmental impacts are poorly understood. To address these gaps and inform effective interventions, the
objectives of this research are to (1) examine racial disparities in the neurobehavioral and social-emotional
impacts of SDB and/or insufficient sleep in non-Latinx Black and non-Latinx White preschoolers and (2) identify
proximal and distal socio-ecological factors linked to these racial disparities in sleep-related outcomes.

title: Rescuing impaired fracture healing by molecular targeting
text:
Pathological fracture calluses are deficient and very often fail to ossify despite anti-cancer
drug therapy, radiation therapy and anti-resorptive agents including Rank:Fc antibody (denosumab) or
bisphosphonates (zoledronate). There is no mechanistic understanding as to why fractures do not heal well in
the presence of certain types of breast cancer cells. We expect to establish a novel mechanism-based
therapeutic paradigm for devastating patients suffering from pathological fractures secondary to breast
cancers, the most common cancer in women and causing fractures.

title: Pathogenesis and Treatment of NUT midline carcinoma
text:
Principal Investigator/Program Director (Last, First, Middle): French, Christopher, Alexander
Project Narrative NUT midline carcinoma is an incurable highly aggressive cancer driven by the
BRD4-NUT oncoprotein that has a median survival of 6.5 months with no effective treatment options.
We predict the proposed studies will identify mechanisms that collaborate with BRD4-NUT to drive
NC growth while blocking differentiaiton that will facilitate precise and effective therapeutic targeting.
The findings will greatly impact treatment of NC and likely other BRD4-dependent cancers.

title: Trophoblast Differentiation
text:
STATEMENT
Disorders of hemochorial placentation are a significant human health issue. There is a paucity of knowledge
regarding the regulation of trophoblast stem cells, their differentiation into invasive/extravillous trophoblast cells
that effectively invade into the uterus and restructure uterine spiral arteries and establish the uterine-placental
interface. Experimental dissection of fundamental mechanisms underlying the derivation of the
invasive/extravillous trophoblast cell lineage is a key to understanding the etiology of placentation-related
diseases and a necessity for establishing appropriate and efficacious diagnostic and therapeutic strategies.

title: Characterizing and Targeting the NUP98 Fusion Oncoprotein Interactome
text:
Oncogenic gene fusions involving Nucleoporin 98 (NUP98) are recurrent in pediatric acute myeloid leukemia
(AML) and are associated with poor patient outcomes. NUP98 fusion oncoproteins localize within the nucleus
in membrane-less organelles, or “puncta”, that are necessary for cell transformation and deregulated gene
expression, and the studies proposed here will interrogate the composition of NUP98 FO-associated puncta
and their potential for therapeutic targeting. By identifying which members of the NUP98 FO interactome are
functionally important and determining if puncta disruption is necessary for therapeutic benefit, this research
plan may identify new therapeutic approaches for high-risk, NUP98-rearranged AMLs.

title: Dissecting mechanisms of molecular convergence and variable expressivity in inborn errors of immunity
text:
Inborn errors of immunity (IEIs) encompass over 500 monogenic disorders that, despite arising from distinct
genetic variants, often converge on shared immunological symptoms such as recurrent infections, allergy, and
malignancy; yet patients with identical pathogenic variants can still exhibit markedly different clinical courses,
the mechanisms of which remain poorly understood. This presents a unique opportunity to identify shared
therapeutic targets across disorders and develop prognostication tools that enable early intervention and thereby
improve clinical outcomes. Here, we have developed cutting-edge cell-engineering and computational methods
to map convergent molecular outputs across diverse IEIs, assess shared therapeutic sensitivity, and identify
genetic modifiers of clinical variability through both patient-cohort analyses and engineered-cell experiments.

title: Selection system for identifying protein-specific folding tags that enable purification of native cytokines from E. coli
text:
Numerous cytokines are needed for cell culture, but most are difficult
and costly to purify. We have developed a powerful method to create folding tags for
recombinant production in E. coli. Folding tags facilitate purification of the key growth
factors needed to create defined, synthetic cell culture media and aid in the reliable and
economical production of therapeutic cells.

title: Quantifying health effects of cannabis use and cannabis use disorder on geriatric syndromes and HIV outcomes: causal effects analysis in the Veterans Aging Cohort Study and the Mt. Sinai HIV Cohort
text:
As stronger cannabis products become more available with cannabis legalization, there is an urgent need to
evaluate and share data on cannabis use and risks among aging people with HIV (PWH) who may be more
susceptible to harm from cannabis use. We will use data from the Veterans Aging Cohort Study and the Mount
Sinai HIV Cohort to: 1) assess how cannabis use and cannabis use disorder is linked to risk of falls, fractures,
delirium, dementia, HIV viral suppression and HIV medication adherence; and 2) build and validate a tool that
allows researchers to use electronic health records to more easily examine cannabis use and study its risks
and benefits. Until cannabis use and cannabis use disorder are universally screened in health care settings
across the U.S., the new tool we build and validate may help health systems rapidly estimate cannabis
exposure in their patients and provide data to guide urgently needed policies for cannabis use disorder
screening, diagnosis, and treatment.

title: The Impact of Diffuse Mild Brain Injury on Clinical Outcomes in Children
text:
Pediatric mild traumatic brain injury (pmTBI) is a common neurological disorder that potentially alters
the health and neurodevelopmental trajectories of millions of children worldwide. Approximately 20-35% of
patients with pmTBI experience long-term (>3 months post-injury) physical, emotional, academic, and social
consequences from their injury. Importantly, the mechanisms underlying diffuse injuries in pmTBI and the
physiological recovery times remain largely unknown. Emerging evidence suggests that advanced imaging and
blood-based biomarkers remain altered months post-injury. The current application directly addresses this major
public health concern through the collection of innovative biomarker and clinical data in a large sample of pmTBI
(N=178) during acute (within 48 hours), sub-acute (3-10 days) and more chronic (4 months) post-injury phases.
An equally powered cohort of healthy controls (N=132) are included so that traumatic injuries can be
disambiguated from typical neurodevelopment (i.e., sex and age-dependent effects).
